segments.t: KTPH000 is the command-line client for korTTY's KTPH001Control APIKTPH002. It ships inside every korTTY package as a second launcher beside the application itself, finds the running korTTY on its own, authenticates, and turns the API's answers into something a shell script or a coding agent can act on.
It talks only to a korTTY running KTPH000on the same computer as youKTPH001, and only while that korTTY has the Control API switched on. Everything the API refuses, the CLI refuses too.

Without KTPH000Settings › Terminal › Control APIKTPH001 ticked there is nothing to connect to, and every command exits with code 3. See KTPH002Control APIKTPH003 for what you are turning on and what it can do.
KTPH000 is not a script — it is a real launcher built into the packaged application image, so it starts the bundled JVM without needing Java on your KTPH001.
KTPH000 — at the image root, not under KTPH001
Only the pacman package puts it on your KTPH000 for you. Everywhere else, add the directory to KTPH001 or link the launcher into a directory that is already on it:

The launcher is deliberately KTPH004notKTPH005 called KTPH000: that name belongs to the graphical launcher (KTPH001 on Arch, KTPH002 elsewhere), and on macOS and Windows, whose filesystems ignore case, a second launcher called KTPH003 would collide with it.
The KTPH000 and KTPH001 archives carry no launchers beyond the graphical one. From those, start the client as KTPH002.

The groups are KTPH000, KTPH001, KTPH002, KTPH003, KTPH004, KTPH005, KTPH006, KTPH007 and KTPH008. Inside a group, a command name is the API method after the dot with its underscores spelled as dashes — KTPH009 is KTPH010. Four methods do not follow from their name and are worth learning: KTPH011 is KTPH012, KTPH013 is KTPH014, KTPH015 is KTPH016, and anything without a command of its own — KTPH017, KTPH018 — is reached through KTPH019.
Everything a command needs is a flag. There are no positional arguments except the key names of KTPH000 and KTPH001, and the method and JSON of KTPH002.

KTPH000 prints the complete machine-readable command surface — every command, its options, its result shape, its errors and a worked example — straight from the running korTTY. The parameters, results and errors come from the same declarations the server dispatches, and each entry's KTPH001 line is checked against this client's own parser before release, so both describe the version you are actually talking to; use it rather than guessing, especially from a script that has to keep working across versions.
Every KTPH000 and KTPH001 command takes KTPH002exactly oneKTPH003 selector, and every selector is a flag:
That pane, which must be unique among the open ones
The pane you are looking at
The pane the command is KTPH000running inKTPH001
Giving none of them, or more than one, is a syntax error (exit 2) that names the four; a bare KTPH000 or KTPH001 written where a flag belongs is a syntax error too.

KTPH000 is resolved by the client, not the server: it walks its own process ancestry and asks korTTY which pane owns one of those process ids. That is why it works from a sub-shell, a KTPH001 recipe or a nested script without any setup, and why it fails loudly with a clear message where it cannot work rather than addressing the wrong pane.

It matches against the operating-system process id of a pane's local shell. Inside an SSH session, inside a container, or in the Flatpak package — where local shells run on the host through KTPH000 and korTTY never sees their process ids — there is nothing to match and KTPH001 cannot resolve. Address the pane explicitly there.

Commands that wait — KTPH000, KTPH001, KTPH002, KTPH003 — block until the condition is met or the timeout expires, and exit 4 on a timeout. Every wait has a server-side hard cap of ten minutes; a longer request is clamped and the answer says so.

Requests on one connection run one at a time, so a script that wants to wait on one pane while doing something in another simply runs two commands concurrently — each opens its own connection. Up to eight connections may be open at once.
KTPH000 subscribes to korTTY's coding-agent events and prints one JSON object per line, as they happen, until it is told to stop.

KTPH000 and KTPH001 take comma-separated lists and narrow what is delivered; KTPH002 adds the detector's evidence to each event; KTPH003 stops after N events. Three things end the stream: KTPH004 is reached, the KTPH005 passes, or you interrupt it. The first two exit 0. An interrupt is KTPH007notKTPH008 handled — there is deliberately no signal handler, so the process ends with the shell's 128 + SIGINT = 130, which is worth allowing for in a CI job that wraps the stream in KTPH006.
With neither KTPH000 nor KTPH001, the stream has no deadline at all and runs until korTTY exits or you stop it.
The exit code comes from the server, not from a table the client keeps, so the two can never disagree.
The request was valid but could not be carried out: no such pane, tab or agent; not connected; the write failed; the last pane cannot be closed
Sometimes — the answer's KTPH000 field says
The request itself was wrong: a bad selector, an unknown key name, an invalid regular expression, a missing or out-of-range parameter, an unknown command
Refused: the Control API is off, enterprise policy denies it, the token was rejected, korTTY is not ready yet, or too many connections are open
KTPH000 was interrupted (Ctrl-C). The stream has no signal handler, so this is the shell's own 128 + SIGINT

Every failure prints a one-line diagnostic on stderr in the form KTPH000, where KTPH001 is the stable wire code — KTPH002, KTPH003, KTPH004 — that the exit code above was derived from. Add KTPH005 to get the whole JSON-RPC error object instead, which is what a script should branch on:

Failures the client diagnoses on its own are the exception: an unparseable command line, a korTTY that is not running, a KTPH000 that matches no pane and an expired client deadline never reached the server, so they carry no wire code and print a bare KTPH001 on either setting. Branch on the exit code for those.
KTPH000 prints the version and exits 0. It is the only command that does KTPH001notKTPH002 need a running korTTY, which makes it the right thing to put in an installation check or a CI smoke test.
Nothing is written to stdout except the command's result, so KTPH000 pipes cleanly.
Diagnostics, warnings and error objects go to stderr.

The authentication token is read from KTPH000 by the client. There is no KTPH001 option and no environment variable, deliberately: a token on a command line ends up in the process list and in your shell history.
korTTY logs one line per action the CLI performs, and raises one desktop notification the first time a program types into a pane. Your script is not invisible, by design.
